storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere nearby this evening — clear skies and no weather alerts, so there's nothing for the Sound to protect the cove from tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Marine layer holds at 4 PM (9°F air–water gap) but fades around 5:15 PM and is gone by 6 PM as the air cools below the 60°F Sound — no buffer this evening, though none is needed.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: Quiet. The Upton (KOKX) radar shows no precipitation echoes in range, there are no NWS watches, warnings, or advisories, and the atmosphere has no storm fuel at all — CAPE (a measure of how much energy rising air has to build thunderstorms) is 0 J/kg. Winds aloft are a moderate 24 kt from the west-northwest, but with zero instability that shear has nothing to organize.

Local modifier: The cool Sound sometimes acts as a shield for the cove — when the water is well below the air, a stable, cool layer sits over it and tends to weaken storms coming off the land. At 4 PM that gap is about 9°F (air ~70°F, Sound ~60°F). But the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools after sunset, so the protective gap closes: the model projects it dropping below the ~5°F threshold around 5:15 PM, to about 1°F by 6 PM, and by 7–8 PM the air is actually colder than the water (2–4°F below). Any storm arriving this evening would find no buffer at all.

Most likely outcome: Dry, clear evening for the cove and surrounding towns alike. With nothing on radar and no instability, there is no meaningful difference between the shoreline and inland areas tonight.

What would change the call: Only an unexpected development of showers to the west, which the current data gives no hint of. The model forecast beyond 8 PM was unavailable this run, but with no fuel in the atmosphere and a dry westerly flow, a late-evening surprise is very unlikely.

wind.regime_label: Light westerly gradient — no sea breeze, fading after sunset
wind.tactics_blurb: Light westerly that backs toward WSW after the 5:57 PM sunset — no sea breeze to organize it, so expect 4–5 kt with soft spots near the Connecticut shore. Stay center, keep the boat moving, and head toward the mouth of the cove where the westerly comes in less blocked by land.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of day it is: light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander. The ingredients for a sea breeze were half there: the air–water temperature difference was a healthy 9.4°F this afternoon (warm land, 60°F Sound), but the sea breeze never formed — only 2 of 19 shoreline stations show any southerly component, and the whole region from Rye to Westerly is blowing west. With sunset at 5:57 PM, essentially the whole 5–10 PM window is after dark, so there's no thermal left to wait for anyway.

Wind strength: The background wind across the western Sound is light — western-Sound airports average about 5 kt and the HRRR model holds the cove at 4–5 kt all evening. Riverside YC is currently reading a 10-minute average of 8 kt with puffs to 13 kt out of the WNW, but that's late-afternoon mixing from the warm land; as the air cools after sunset it stabilizes near the surface and those gusts die off. Expect 5 kt at the start, easing to about 4 kt by 9–10 PM. Stronger breeze exists farther east (12 kt at Groton and Block Island), but it isn't reaching this end of the Sound.

Direction and where the pressure is: Westerly near 280° at 5 PM, backing to west-southwest (240–260°) after sunset. A westerly blows down the Sound from the New York end — the direction is usually steady, but it tends to leave holes along the Connecticut shore while staying stronger out in the open Sound. In the cove that means lighter, patchier air near the docks and the western shore, and slightly better pressure toward the mouth. There's no strong side to commit to, so the call is center, leaning toward the open water.

Shift character: Not a classic oscillating breeze. In wind this light, expect slow, wandering shifts of 10–20° rather than a regular rhythm, plus a gradual leftward drift (backing) through the evening. Play the pressure more than the shifts — a puff is worth more than a 10° lift tonight.

What racers will feel: Drifter-class conditions for much of the fleet — enough to sail at the start, marginal by the end. Heavier boats will struggle; light-air technique and keeping the boat moving matter most. The model forecast beyond 8 PM was unavailable this run, so the 9 and 10 PM numbers are extrapolated from the trend.
